Con esto se hace una votación verificabl: With this a verifiable vote can be held. Each voter encrypts their vote, 0 or 1, with the polling board's public key. Anybody can multiply all the ciphertexts and obtain the ciphertext of the sum, that is, of the number of yeses, without decrypting a single vote. Only at the end does the board, with the private key, decrypt that single result: the count. No individual vote is ever opened.

El cifrado de Paillier, de 1999, es homo: Paillier's cipher, from 1999, is homomorphic for addition: the product of two ciphertexts is the ciphertext of the sum of the messages. It works modulo $n^2$, with $n = pq$ as in RSA, and it has another property that is key for voting: it is probabilistic, each ciphertext carries a random number, so two equal votes give different ciphertexts and nobody can tell who voted what by comparing envelopes.
El cifrado totalmente homomórfico (Gentr: Fully homomorphic encryption (Gentry, 2009) adds and multiplies without limit: it computes any function on encrypted data, still slowly.

El producto de los dos cifrados, módulo: The product of the two ciphertexts, modulo 1225.
El voto electrónico verificable usa cifr: Verifiable electronic voting uses homomorphic encryption in real trials, such as some ballots in Estonia and Switzerland: the encrypted ballot box is published and anybody checks the count without seeing the votes. Analytics companies offer to process encrypted medical or genetic data without decrypting it, so that neither they nor an attacker who breaks in sees the data. And systems that train models on data from several hospitals without pooling it in the clear rest on these techniques along with Shamir's secret sharing.

Hasta ahora, para hacer algo con un dato: Until now, to do anything with an encrypted item you had to decrypt it, and that forces you to trust whoever holds the key. Homomorphic encryption breaks that rule: it allows operations on the ciphertexts such that the result, when decrypted, is the operation on the messages. A server can add, or even compute anything at all, on data it cannot read.
La idea usa retículos, como la criptogra: The idea uses lattices, like the post-quantum cryptography of the next topic, and it has a problem: each operation adds “noise” to the ciphertext, and past a point the noise makes decryption impossible. Gentry added a brilliant step, bootstrapping, which reduces the noise by encrypting the decryption itself. It works, but it is slow: millions of times slower than computing in the clear. Today it is used in particular cases, medical or financial analysis on data that cannot be seen, and it improves year by year.
La maleabilidad de [[cr-rsa|RSA]] era un: [[cr-rsa|RSA]]'s malleability was a defect: multiplying ciphertexts multiplied messages. This topic turns that defect into a tool. With the usual [[cr-modular|modular arithmetic]], a cipher in which adding the ciphertexts adds the messages makes it possible to count votes without opening a single envelope.

Ronald Rivest, Leonard Adleman y Michael: Ronald Rivest, Leonard Adleman and Michael Dertouzos posed the question in 1978, the year after RSA: can you compute on encrypted data? Pascal Paillier gave in 1999 the additive cipher that bears his name.
